title: Circuit Claims Depend on What Is Extracted and How It Is Compared
claim: Reported overlap and rankings depend on what is extracted and how it is compared, and behavior gains track recruited extra components.
layout: 3 panels in 2x2 grid (A spans top), lettered, dot plots with value labels
description: A multi-panel figure of three empirical plots, each with a bold lettered title. Panel A, across the top, has two side-by-side dot plots with 95% confidence-interval bars. They compare Jaccard@10 overlap for Success and Near-miss cases. Left: selected attention heads, with deterministic ties in blue circles at about 0.55–0.67 and random ties in orange diamonds near 0.03. Right: connection groups, with observed overlap in blue and a gray score-weighted baseline, both near 0.14–0.16. Numeric labels sit at the right of each row. Panel B, bottom left, is a dumbbell plot of node-fraction gaps for three graph types, with circles for moderate and squares for extensive. Panel C, bottom right, is a scatter of bridge fraction against RL compositional accuracy gain, with green annotated points and gray or open markers for baselines.
caption: Overview of the three ﬁndings. A: attention-head and structural edge-bundle overlap at the denseversus-75%-sparse RL comparison. Circles show observed means; error bars show 95% bootstrap conﬁdence intervals over 16 matched task–object entries per split. Diamonds show means for random tie handling (heads) or the score-weighted random baseline (connection groups). B: node-fraction gaps for curriculum-initialized RL, comparing repeated core extractions and joint versus separate query/key representations of the other two graphs (pruning loss budget τ = 0.12). C: compositional-task exact-match accuracy gain versus core-circuit bridge fraction across RL initialization conditions. Open Atomic-only symbols mark upper bounds on compositional accuracy gain. In B and C, circles and squares denote the moderately and extensively expanded distributions, respectively. Values in B are moderate/extensive.
abstract: Circuit extraction identifies model components whose presence preserves a target behavior under ablation, but preserving behavior does not single out one circuit. We study this in a synthetic Lean tactic-prediction benchmark with fixed proof rules and randomized surface form. Across dense and weight-sparse checkpoints of the same transformer, evaluated on atomic and compositional proofs, we vary which extracted object is reported: a compact prediction-preserving circuit, a broader graph retaining surrounding read, write, and routing structure, or a subgraph extracted with a post-ablation loss budget. First, overlap between groups of component-to-component connections is low, sometimes close to a random baseline. Overlap is much higher for selected attention-head sets under deterministic selection, but falls sharply when selection among equally scored heads is randomized. Second, the normalized graph-size ranking of conditions that differ in which supervised checkpoint initializes reinforcement learning (RL) agrees between repeated extractions of the compact circuit and between joint and separate query/key representations of each of the other two graphs. For the loss-budgeted graph, query/key ordering agreement persists through the budget sweep. Finally, across those same conditions, the largest exact-match accuracy gains from RL on compositional proofs come with the largest proportion of components in the compositional circuit that lie outside the corresponding atomic circuits. Ablating these additional components in the sparse RL model reduces compositional accuracy while largely preserving accuracy on the corresponding atomic tasks. A circuit-level claim therefore requires specifying which circuit is reported and how it is extracted and compared; behavior alone does not determine its interpretation. We distill these requirements into a reporting practice for circuit-extraction studies.
